newsitem.title: USA: N.Y stiffens penalties for evading cigarette taxes.
newsitem.headline: N.Y stiffens penalties for evading cigarette taxes.

text.p: New York State Gov. George Pataki made it harder for retailers to evade cigarette taxes, signing a bill to revoke their lottery and alcoholic beverage licenses if they possess or sell contraband cigarettes.

The new law also increased fines for retailers who fail to register with the state by five times to $1,000, and imposed a civil fine of the same amount for a first offense of continuing to sell cigarettes after a license is revoked.
Other measures that were signed into law on September 4 seek to aid cities and municipalities, by making them more competitive and lowering their costs.

New York City's tax laws were reformed to phase out the "income-plus-compensation" alternative tax base for corporations, which required them to add back officers' salaries and other compensation to their tax base.
About 18,000 corporations are expected to benefit, according to the city.
The exemption level for companies that pay the income-plus-compensation alternative tax was raised to $40,000 from $15,000 over two years, aiding about 38,000 businesses.

New York City's "place of business" requirement was eliminated so that companies that do not have a location outside the city but ship goods out of its jurisdiction do not suffer a competitive disadvantage.

And the last part of the bill lets manuracturers opt to "double weight" the receipts part of their business allocation formula, to offset the tax burden companies with large numbers of workers and property face.

Other new laws will let counties consolidate special improvement districts. And municipalities will be able to enter cooperation agreements for up to five years or the period of "probable usefulness" for debt issued with the agreement.
This law aims to allow the local governments to better fund long-term projects, like capital improvements.
In another move to save money for municipalities, the new rules add an exception to competitive bidding requirements, allowing for "cooperative purchasing."
Municipalities now will be allowed to buy materials, equipment or supplies, or to contract for services through the county in which they are located or through an adjoining county.
